title: Experimentally mapped aggregation-critical protein regions, with circularity, prediction-concordance and training-set-contamination labels
description:
A hand-curated set of 27 protein regions across 17 proteins, shown experimentally to be required for, or to constitute the core of, protein aggregation. Every row was established by opening the source paper and checking the claim against it.

NEW IN 1.5.0, AND READ THIS BEFORE CITING AN EARLIER VERSION: a residue range is corrected. DISC1’s deleted region is 384-414, not 384-415. Every version from 1.0.0 to 1.4.0 records the wrong value. The correction comes from the corresponding author of the source, by email on 19 November 2026, and rests on sequencing of the actual plasmids: the construct joins DISC1 1-383 to DISC1 415-854, which leaves 384-414 absent — 31 residues, not 32. The value this dataset had recorded came from plasmid names in a PhD thesis table, and those names disagree with the sequencing of those same plasmids.

Also new in 1.5.0: six rows, a new core column, and the useful result that the six rows changed nothing. Added are CHCHD10 42-75, CHCHD2 54-86, TAF15 7-99, Orb2 176-206 (Drosophila), beta-2-microglobulin 22-85 and SOD1 3-55,86-153. Four of the six are the first rows in this dataset whose stratum was assigned before the modern predictor ran on them, verifiable from the repository’s commit history rather than asserted. And the usable confirmatory cell is still 2 rows. Three of the six proteins are in CPAD; five of the six rows cannot return a significant result for any predictor; SOD1 is a discontinuous core and can carry no statistic at all. That is the finding, not a disappointment: the rows that are easy to add are systematically the rows that cannot discriminate between predictors. The new column, power_eligible, is what makes that visible — see below.

The dataset carries four columns that aggregation datasets usually lack, each because omitting it produces a benchmark that silently measures the wrong thing:

  • construct — which construct established the region. A region can be necessary in one construct and dispensable in another, and both results can be correct.
  • circularity_status — whether a predictor was in the discovery path. A region found by a predictor cannot be used to test that predictor. Circular rows are kept and labelled, not dropped.
  • stratum — whether experiment and prediction agree. Regions that are mapped cleanly tend to be the ones predictors find, so a dataset of well-mapped regions is enriched for agreement; only discordant rows can discriminate between predictors.
  • cpad_status — new in 1.1.0. Whether the row's protein is in CPAD 2.0, and therefore whether a modern predictor's hit on it may be recall of training data rather than prediction. This is a third kind of circularity, distinct from the discovery path and from experiment–prediction agreement.

The contamination check was the main change in 1.1.0, and its result is sobering. All 27 rows carry it — each checked against all three CPAD 2.0 datasets, read complete, plus an orthologue check in both OMA and OrthoInspector, because the CPAD90 training set transfers annotations to homologues. Nine of the seventeen proteins are CPAD members. Of the sixteen rows in the discordant family — the only stratum that can discriminate between predictors — five are CPAD-contaminated and eleven are not. A reader benchmarking a modern predictor on this dataset without that column would measure memorisation on most of the rows that appear to matter.

New in 1.2.0: four rows, and a negative result about this dataset's own growth. Added are ANXA11 39-74, TMEM106B 120-254, glycinin G4 164-190 — the first non-animal row, a plant seed storage protein — and a DISC1 interval split into the two sub-intervals its source actually tested. The dataset grew from 17 rows to 21 and the usable discordant stratum did not move off 2 rows. That is worth stating plainly for anyone planning to extend it: row count is not the scarce resource. A row can only enter the discordant stratum if its source paper ran an aggregation predictor on the region and reported it disagreeing with the experiment, and most structural papers never run one at all — which is why 6 of 27 rows still carry stratum: PENDING rather than a verdict, one of them permanently. Extending this dataset usefully means searching methods sections for reported predictor failures, not searching for more proteins with mapped cores.

New in 1.4.0: a structure column, and the first result this dataset was used to predict in advance. Seven rows describe the ordered core of a deposited fibril structure, and each now records which PDB entry, which chain, which candidates were considered and the rule that chose among them. Its absence is informative too: it means no fibril structure exists for that row, which is the case for every DISC1 and TRIOBP-1 row and is why those rows cannot enter any structure-based analysis.

A CORE-POLARITY RESULT WAS REPORTED WITH VERSION 1.4.0 AND IS WITHDRAWN AS OF VERSION 1.5.0. Using the seven rows that then had a deposited structure, a measure of how polar the buried fibril core is was specified in writing — including the condition under which it would be abandoned — before any coordinate was read, and it gave Spearman ρ = +0.82 (exact one-sided p = 0.017) against how badly a modern predictor recovered the region. A pre-registered control run on 20 November 2026 withdrew the structural reading of that number. The polar fraction of the region’s own SEQUENCE — which needs no structure at all — predicts the same outcome BETTER: ρ = +0.89, p = 0.0062. The two quantities are collinear at ρ = +0.96, and once sequence composition is controlled for, the structural measure’s residual association is NEGATIVE. The association is real and is compositional, not structural, and it is not new: Louros et al. (2020), Nat Commun 11:3314, established it five years earlier at far larger n. The measurements stand; the interpretation placed on them does not.

THE MEASURE ITSELF WAS ALSO NOT NEW, WHICH IS A SEPARATE PROBLEM FROM THE ONE ABOVE. Found by a prior-art audit on 19 November 2026. García-Pardo et al. (2023), Nature Communications 14:239, doi:10.1038/s41467-023-35854-0, tabulate “the percentage of buried polar residues” for six fibril structures, computed with PDBePISA. The overlap is numerical, not merely conceptual: their hSAA1 entry is PDB 6MST residues 2-55, the identical entry and range as this dataset’s serum amyloid A row. They publish 46%; this project computes 0.4615 by a different burial definition. Two independent implementations agreeing to within 0.2 percentage points is a validation, and it is reported here as one. What is this project’s own is the operationalisation — a reproducible script rather than a web server, edge-free burial by helical replication rather than a deposited five-rung model, 22 structures with a calibrated AUROC rather than a six-structure descriptive table — and the use of the measure as a covariate on predictor output, which is a separate claim.

It had been fragile before it was withdrawn, and the fragility is worth recording. Dropping any one of four of the seven proteins moved p above 0.05; two of the seven structures reverse order between the two pre-registered burial cutoffs; and at the OTHER registered cutoff the headline correlation is ρ = +0.68, p = 0.0548 — it fails the project’s own threshold at its own alternative setting. It could also never have spoken to the dataset’s headline question, because the two proteins the project was built around have no deposited fibril structures at all. The full specification, the control, the decision rule that was committed before the control was computed, and every number above are in the repository. They are left in place rather than deleted, because a withdrawn claim with its reasoning intact is more useful to a reader than a gap.

New in 1.3.0: seven stratum labels, and a flag saying which of them count. Seven rows sat at stratum: PENDING while the legacy predictor had already been run on them. The project's pre-registration says the label comes from published predictor results where they exist and otherwise from the legacy run itself, so the rule was applied: six rows became DISCORDANT and one CONCORDANT, by a fixed threshold chosen before any score existed. But the pre-registration also fixes an ORDER — label first, then run the modern predictor — and that order had already been broken, so each relabelled row carries stratum_assignment.confirmatory_eligible: false. The confirmatory set is unchanged at 2 rows. This is recorded rather than quietly fixed because a reader benchmarking against this dataset needs to know which labels were assigned blind and which were not. A new column, stratum_assignment, carries the rule, the legacy score it was applied to, and the previous value for every affected row.

And a caution on counting rows, which 1.5.0 makes sharper. The eleven discordant, CPAD-absent, circularity-clean rows span eight proteins: three are intervals of one protein and two of another, and CHCHD10 and CHCHD2 are a further non-independent pair. Tests that assume independent observations should treat the protein, not the row, as the unit.

AND A HARDER LIMIT, WHICH THE NEW power_eligible COLUMN MAKES EXPLICIT. Tile a chain into non-overlapping 6-residue windows: M of them, m inside the mapped region. Under the null, the chance that the chain’s top-ranked window falls inside the region is exactly m/M — so m/M is the smallest p a statistic reading the region’s best window rank can return for that row, whatever predictor is used. 15 of the 27 rows exceed the 0.05 bar, and for them no predictor and no better predictor can produce a significant result; only a longer protein or a shorter mapped region would. This bites hardest exactly where new rows are easiest to find: of the 13 rows describing a deposited fibril core, one is eligible, because an ordered core is a large fraction of a short construct and eligibility requires the opposite. The general result — setting aside hypotheses that cannot reject at the nominal level under a discrete null — is Gart, Chu & Tarone (1979), J Natl Cancer Inst 62:957-974, and Mantel (1980), Biometrics 36:381-399, the latter attributing the remark to John Tukey. CORRECTED 20 November 2026, AFTER THIS VERSION WAS DEPOSITED. The deposited DATA_DESCRIPTOR.md cites Tarone (1990) for this, which is how the significant-pattern-mining literature names it but is not where the idea appears: Tarone’s own introduction attributes the exclusion to Gart et al. and to Mantel, and his paper’s own contribution is a sharper multiplicity correction that this project does not use. Deposited files are frozen and this description is not, so the correction is stated here. What is new remains only the application, and it differs from the originals in purpose: they set aside untestable hypotheses to shrink a multiplicity correction, this dataset does so to say a benchmark row is uninformative in principle. A rank-sum statistic has a different and lower floor, 1/C(M,m), which limits how broadly the claim may be stated but rescues none of these rows.

A caution on re-scoring, new in 1.2.0. Every row carries a frame, and the frame is not a formality: scoring a region inside a frame that contains a hydrophobic segment which was never in the sample — a signal peptide, a transmembrane helix — makes every predictor look worse, because such a segment scores highly and is right to. Glycinin G4 is the worked example: its precursor carries a 23-residue signal peptide, so the row is framed on the mature A4 chain that actually aggregated. Re-scoring these rows in a different frame will give different numbers for that reason and no other.

Limitations are stated in the data descriptor and should be read before use. The dataset is small and is not a random sample. The funnel, in the order the pre-registration applies it: 27 rows → 16 in the discordant family → 11 after excluding CPAD members → 11 after excluding circular rows → 5 after excluding labels assigned once the modern scores were known → 2 after excluding rows no rank-based statistic could ever pass. The two survivors are TRIOBP-1 324-348 and DISC1 384-414. That supports a case series on two proteins, not a rate. The dataset grew by six rows and that number did not move. The rows excluded at the last two steps are usable and are labelled, so a reader can tell which kind of exclusion applies — and the two kinds must not be pooled: one is a procedural defect of ours, the other is arithmetic. 6 of 27 rows are not yet assessed for stratum, one of them permanently, because no statistic is defined for a discontinuous core. Rows are not independent. Most rows are recombinant or cell-based and cannot speak to aggregation in patients. The CPAD90 membership list is unpublished, so no row can be certified training-set-clean in absolute terms.
